claims.claim: Frank Mentzer's redline review of the Quagmire! rough draft objected that the text was padded.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire! The Making of a 1980's D&D Module', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: obviously padded
claims.page: Development Hell Level 7: Rough Draft Consultation

claims.claim: Mentzer's review of the same draft also faulted it as extremely repetitive.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire! The Making of a 1980's D&D Module', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: extremely repetitive

claims.claim: Mentzer objected to the redundant construction 'Patriarch Cleric' by likening it to 'female girl'.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014, reporting Mentzer's marginalia
claims.quote: female girl

claims.claim: Mentzer's consultation role was to ensure BECMI modules used the game's system terms consistently.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: exercised the system consistently

claims.claim: Every TSR module of the period had a product standards sheet fixing its styles, type sizes and margins.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: listed all of the styles, typesizes, margins

claims.claim: Much of the flavor text that troubled Mentzer was cut from the published module.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: including the saving throw notation and the flavor text

claims.claim: The module's section breakdown worksheet projected each section's length in both pages and lines of the HP3000 editor.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: measured both by page count and by line count
claims.page: Development Hell Level 5: Design Crunch Time

claims.claim: TSR stripped city names from the player-facing map of Quagmire!, and withheld the pointer to the Spiral City itself.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: is withheld from the players
claims.page: Development Hell Level 6: Maps and Illustrations

claims.claim: The front cover of a 1984 TSR module carried only a few sentences of flavor text beneath the cover illustration.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, 'Quagmire!', Medium, 2014
claims.quote: a few sentences of flavor text
claims.confidence: medium: the phrase describes the cover blurb, not interior read-aloud text

claims.claim: Garcia read and compared more than 5,500 pages of D&D and Pathfinder rulebook text across editions for his 2017 study.
claims.source: Antero Garcia, Mind, Culture, and Activity 24(3), 2017
claims.quote: more than 5,500 pages

claims.claim: The 1989 AD&D second edition defended its exclusive male pronoun as clear, concise and familiar in written material.
claims.source: David 'Zeb' Cook, AD&D 2nd ed. (1989) p. 9, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: clear, concise, and familiar
claims.page: Gender construction and representation in D&D, p. 238

claims.claim: Garcia reports that D&D rulebooks stopped explaining their pronoun choice from the third edition (2000) onward.
claims.source: Antero Garcia, Mind, Culture, and Activity 24(3), 2017
claims.quote: Explanations about pronouns would cease with later editions

claims.claim: The 5e Player's Handbook tells the reader that nine human ethnic groups are widely recognized in the Forgotten Realms.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 30, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: nine human ethnic groups are widely recognized

claims.claim: The same 5e passage frames material culture and physical characteristics as varying by region.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 30, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: change wildly from region to region

claims.claim: The 5e half-orc entry carries a bolded named paragraph, 'Grudging Acceptance', describing how half-orcs are received by others.
claims.source: D&D 5e Player's Handbook (2014) p. 41, quoted by Antero Garcia (2017)
claims.quote: Grudging Acceptance

claims.claim: Gygax described Holmes's contribution to the 1977 Basic Set as the rewriting and editing that extracted a beginner's set from existing D&D texts.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, Dragon #14 (May 1978), compiled by Zach Howard, Zenopus Archives, 2013
claims.quote: the rewriting and editing necessary to extract a

claims.claim: Gygax said TSR decided the original booklets needed a clarified introductory piece for a wider readership.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, Dragon #35 (March 1980), compiled by Zach Howard, Zenopus Archives, 2013
claims.quote: clarified, introductory piece was needed

claims.claim: An RPGA interviewer in 1981 characterised Holmes's Basic Set as easier reading than the original set and Mentzer's as understandable by anyone willing to read it.
claims.source: RPGA interviewer (presumed Frank Mentzer), Polyhedron #1 (1981), compiled by Zach Howard
claims.quote: a little bit easier
claims.confidence: medium: the compiler marks the interviewer's identity as presumed

claims.claim: Gygax judged Holmes's editorial work on the Basic Set favourably in a 2005 forum reply.
claims.source: Gary Gygax, EN World post 22 Feb 2005, compiled by Zach Howard
claims.quote: fine bit of editing with the set

claims.claim: Trammell argues the aim of the orientalist register is encyclopedic knowledge of an imagined other.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016
claims.quote: produce encyclopedic knowledge about an imagined and exotic other
claims.page: image caption, section on Orientalist texts

claims.claim: Trammell criticises the reductionism by which one sourcebook is written as if a whole culture could be contained by a single text.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016
claims.quote: contained by a single text

claims.claim: Trammell shows Oriental Adventures gives elite occupations far more specific named detail than commoner ones.
claims.source: Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies III:1, January 2016
claims.quote: the culture of the common people is barely distinguishable

claims.claim: A reader commenting on Trammell's essay attributes Oriental Adventures' authorship to David Cook on the evidence of its diction and style.
claims.source: Commenter on Aaron Trammell, Analog Game Studies, comment thread
claims.quote: Judging from the diction and style of the writing
claims.confidence: low: an unverified reader comment, offered here only as evidence that readers hear an author-specific house voice

claims.claim: Merwin advises putting information useful to the DM but not for players into an appendix.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Outlines and Frameworks', D&D Beyond, 9 Oct 2019
claims.quote: not meant to be seen by the players

claims.claim: Merwin tells writers to ask which encounter elements are better shown on a map than described in prose.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Outlines and Frameworks', D&D Beyond, 9 Oct 2019
claims.quote: better represented in a map rather than strictly described in the text

claims.claim: For sandbox adventures Merwin recommends a less detailed encounter description leaning on the NPCs' resources so the DM can set it in any of several places.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer', D&D Beyond, 2020
claims.quote: a less-detailed description that relies on place
claims.confidence: medium: the sentence as published appears to drop a word ('relies less on place'); the following sentence about mountain pass, city streets or abandoned mines carries the sense

claims.claim: Merwin makes the test of an adventure's layout whether it serves the DM running it at the table.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Thinking Like a Designer', D&D Beyond, 2020
claims.quote: serves the DM who will be running your content

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Gygax's own Castle Greyhawk key gave most rooms a one-line note.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: he usually wrote a 1-line note for each room

claims.claim: Judges Guild's Bob Bledsaw said referees told him they wanted only a skeletal framework of description.
claims.source: Bob Bledsaw, Dragon #27, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: a very skeletal framework

claims.claim: Hartlage credits Gygax's longer location descriptions in G1 Steading of the Hill Giant Chief (1978) with setting the pattern for later adventures.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: set the pattern for virtually every adventure to follow

claims.claim: Hartlage identifies the padding mechanism: the convention of long descriptions makes authors stretch a good middle sentence to an assigned length.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length

claims.claim: Hartlage argues a location's length of description should follow its purpose in play, so a sheriff's kitchen needs no inventory.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: no one needs an item-by-item inventory of her kitchen
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage warns that excess description buries the details that would actually enter play.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: An avalanche of description does more than squander page count
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage's defence of boxed text is that it consolidates and marks which features need describing.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: consolidates and identifies features that require description

claims.claim: Hartlage observes that Storm King's Thunder (2016) omits almost all read-aloud text, unlike Curse of Strahd which boxes every location.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: omits almost all read-aloud text

claims.claim: Michael Curtis describes the one-page-dungeon style of Stonehell as giving the minimum information needed to run the dungeon.
claims.source: Michael Curtis, quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2016
claims.quote: the minimum amount of information needed to run the dungeon

claims.claim: Hartlage's rule for a dungeon key is that descriptions carry telling details and plot-critical information.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 21 Nov 2016
claims.quote: focus on telling details and plot-critical information

claims.claim: B11 King's Festival (1989) told DMs that good description goes beyond sight to noises, smells and touch.
claims.source: Carl Sargent, B11 King's Festival (TSR, 1989), quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
claims.quote: A good DM details more than simply what PCs see
claims.page: B11 King's Festival (1989) — Description and the senses

claims.claim: Keep on the Shadowfell (2008) told DMs to distinguish NPCs with an accent or favourite saying, a signature object, or a single personality adjective.
claims.source: Bruce Cordell and Mike Mearls, H1 Keep on the Shadowfell (2008), paraphrased with a quoted adjective list by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
claims.quote: greedy, bored, suspicious, tired, enthusiastic
claims.confidence: medium: the quoted string is the adventure's adjective list as reproduced by Hartlage, the rest of the sentence is his paraphrase

claims.claim: DDA2 Legions of Thyatis (1990) advised characterising an NPC by picturing him as an animal while describing him.
claims.source: John Nephew, DDA2 Legions of Thyatis (TSR, 1990), quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
claims.quote: visualize him as an animal
claims.page: DDA2 Legions of Thyatis (1990) — Characterizing NPCs

claims.claim: The Hidden Halls of Hazacor (2018) told new DMs to replace unimportant sequences with a short summary.
claims.source: Scott Fitzgerald Gray, The Hidden Halls of Hazacor (2018), quoted by David Hartlage, DMDavid, 2024
claims.quote: you can give the players a short summary instead
claims.page: The Hidden Halls of Hazacor (2018) — Summarize the boring parts

claims.claim: Hartlage notes that the 1999 introductory modules printed scripted text for the DM to read to new players.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 30 Jan 2024, on Eye of the Wyvern (1999)
claims.quote: scripted text for the DM to read to new players

claims.claim: Hartlage describes a fourth-edition design goal of letting a casual DM simply buy an adventure and read its boxed text.
claims.source: David Hartlage, DMDavid, 14 Feb 2023
claims.quote: buy an adventure, read the boxed text
claims.page: Skill challenges satisfied three design goals

claims.claim: McKenzie dates the first appearance of boxed read-aloud text in D&D to the 1980 module The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 18 Dec 2023
claims.quote: marks its first appearance
claims.page: section on descriptive text and 'at rise' descriptions

claims.claim: McKenzie argues D&D read-aloud text is the genre analogue of the theatre's 'at rise' stage description.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 18 Dec 2023
claims.quote: Read-aloud text is analogous to

claims.claim: The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan's own instruction is that its read-aloud text hints at what may be done and that the DM answer questions only vaguely.
claims.source: Harold Johnson and Jeff R. Leason, The Hidden Shrine of Tamoachan (1980), quoted by Brian McKenzie (2023)
claims.quote: the DM should only provide vague information if questioned

claims.claim: McKenzie's summary of the function of read-aloud text is that it offers clues and frames narrative boundaries.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 18 Dec 2023
claims.quote: It offers clues and the frames narrative boundaries

claims.claim: McKenzie states that Jennifer Grouling Cover's is perhaps the only academic discussion of read-aloud text in tabletop adventures.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 18 Dec 2023
claims.quote: one of the few—perhaps the only—academic discussions

claims.claim: Michael Shea likens read-aloud text to the script of a Broadway show.
claims.source: Michael Shea, quoted by Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023
claims.quote: our read-aloud text is part of our script

claims.claim: A Twitter poll by D&D lead rules designer Jeremy Crawford drew 2,248 replies, of which 59.5% wanted occasional boxed text, 34.4% wanted lots and 6% wanted none.
claims.source: Jeremy Crawford's poll, reported by Brian McKenzie, Analog Game Studies, 2023
claims.quote: 2,248 replies
claims.confidence: medium: a self-selected Twitter poll relayed by McKenzie, not a sampled survey

claims.claim: Merwin calls boxed text as much a part of D&D's history and brand as saving throws, hit points and armor class.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: as much a part of D&D's history and brand

claims.claim: Merwin says the act of writing boxed text forces designers to think harder about their encounters.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond, 2019
claims.quote: to think harder about their encounters

claims.claim: A scholarly case study lists read-aloud text, player handouts, DM instructions and NPC dialogue among the five textual elements that carry an adventure's ideas.
claims.source: Brian McKenzie, Bret Zawilski and James Beirne, International Journal of Role-Playing 17, 2026
claims.quote: read-aloud text, player handouts, instructions to the Dungeon Master

claims.claim: Huddleston notes that many early tabletop rulebooks contain little prose or narrative, being given over to rules.
claims.source: Stefan Huddleston, Analog Game Studies, 18 Dec 2022
claims.quote: many early examples lack prose and narrative in favor of rules

claims.claim: Hewitt argues that a Curse of Strahd room's gothic atmosphere is established by the physical objects in its description rather than by naming the mood.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 15 Dec 2024
claims.quote: gothic atmosphere is clearly set through the daunting presence of the statue
claims.confidence: medium: Hewitt names the statue and the skeletal remains as the carriers; the inference that mood is never named is mine unless the verifier reads the surrounding sentences

claims.claim: Hewitt finds Strahd's suggested descriptions unchanged between texts even where his alignment changed.
claims.source: Meghan Hewitt, Analog Game Studies, 15 Dec 2024
claims.quote: descriptions do not change from one text to the other

claims.claim: Hines contrasts Gygax's counterintuitive trap style with fifth edition's preference for clarity in description.
claims.source: Mark Hines, Analog Game Studies, 19 Mar 2023
claims.quote: style of heroism and clarity in description
claims.page: section on Tomb of Horrors and OSR mechanics

claims.claim: Peterson reports that economics dominate the events reported in Arneson's 1971 in-world campaign newsletter.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: Economics play a large role in the events described

claims.claim: The items Peterson lists from that newsletter are civic and financial: a tax collection, restitution paid for damage done by a wizard's dragon's offspring, and a ruined tavern.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: pays restitution for damages caused by his dragon

claims.claim: Peterson says the earliest Blackmoor campaign newsletter tells little about the game system but much about the setting and the state of the campaign.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 3 Aug 2012
claims.quote: significant insight into the setting and the state of the campaign

claims.claim: Peterson dates the earliest explicit use of 'immersion' he has found to Pieter Roos in The Wild Hunt #15 (1977).
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 31 Jan 2021
claims.quote: The earliest explicit use I've found was that of Pieter Roos

claims.claim: Peterson identifies Mike Carr's B1 tips as connecting playing your character's role with a call to immerse yourself in the game setting.
claims.source: Jon Peterson, Playing at the World, 31 Jan 2021, on Mike Carr's B1 (1979)
claims.quote: immerse yourself in the game setting

claims.claim: Alexander's verdict on the form is that location keys in published adventures are almost universally terrible.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 19 May 2014
claims.quote: almost universally terrible

claims.claim: Alexander describes the 1974 sample map's key as instructional rather than practical.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: instructional rather than practical
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Alexander says Gygax's undivided 'wall of text' key remained the TSR staple for the better part of a decade.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: a staple at TSR for the better part of a decade
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Bob Blake's 1976 Judges Guild keys split each entry with a 'DM Only' section, which Alexander reads as structurally the same move as later boxed text.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: section in each key entry
claims.page: A Brief History of the Key

claims.claim: Alexander reports that in the original Lost Tamoachan the read-aloud passages were set in quotation marks, and only the 1980 reissue put them in a box.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: instead appearing between quotation marks

claims.claim: Alexander defines the function of boxed text as marking what a character entering the area learns immediately.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: should be immediately shared with any PC entering the area

claims.claim: The third edition standard format introduced by The Sunless Citadel fixed a set of bold-faced sections that had to appear in one order.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: they appeared in that order and no other

claims.claim: Alexander identifies the failure mode of a fixed section format as filling the format, writing paragraphs where nothing needed saying.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: so you might as well write two or three paragraphs about it

claims.claim: Alexander argues the order of a location's description must follow what is salient there, an ogre in the open being named first and a hidden goblin not.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: should talk about the ogre first

claims.claim: Alexander calls the fourth edition delve format the culmination of rigid formatting and says such a format forces information out of sequence.
claims.source: Justin Alexander, 'The Art of the Key', The Alexandrian, 2014
claims.quote: forces information to be presented out-of-sequence
